title: The Paradigm Shift
label: 01 — What is FSAD
text: 01 — What is FSAD The Paradigm Shift FSAD replaces the traditional handoff-heavy SDLC with a tight feedback loop where humans define what and why in markdown — and AI agents handle the how . 🎯 Spec-Driven, Not Code-Driven The specification — written in markdown — is the primary artifact. It's a living document that evolves in real-time during collaborative sessions. Code is a compilation target, not the source of truth. 🤝 Cross-Functional Pods Small teams of 2–4 (PM + UX + Engineer, or PM + 2 Engineers) sit together — physically or virtually — and co-author the spec in real-time. No handoffs. No waiting for the next sprint. 📝 Markdown as Common Language Markdown is lightweight, version-controlled, diff-friendly, and — critically — the native instruction format for AI agents. Every role can read and write it. It bridges the gap between human intent and machine execution. 🤖 Agent-Delegated Execution Once the spec is validated, teams of AI agents — running in parallel via tools like Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI — implement the code. The human role shifts from writing code to reviewing, steering, and verifying agent output. Models forget. Hooks don't. The Hooks principle — see Claude Best Practices › Hooks

title: From Intent to Deployed Feature
label: 02 — The FSAD Workflow
text: 02 — The FSAD Workflow From Intent to Deployed Feature A five-phase loop designed for speed, clarity, and human oversight. Each phase has a clear checkpoint — you don't advance until the current phase is validated. Phase 1 Intent & Discovery PM UX → problem.md Phase 2 Live Spec Session PM UX Eng → spec.md Phase 3 Implementation Planning Eng Agent → plan.md + tasks/ Phase 4 Agent Execution Agent Agent Agent → code + tests Phase 5 Human Review & Ship Eng UX PM → deploy Phase 1 — Intent & Discovery The PM and UX designer define the problem space and user outcomes. They collaborate — often with an AI research assistant — to surface user needs, competitive landscape, and constraints. The output is a concise problem statement in markdown that frames what we're solving and for whom . No solutions yet. problem.md user-stories.md constraints.md Phase 2 — Live Spec Session The entire pod convenes in a real-time collaborative session. The PM contributes business requirements, UX contributes interaction patterns and design decisions, and the Engineer contributes technical feasibility and architecture. They co-author the spec in markdown together — design decisions are embedded inline, not deferred to a separate Figma-to-Jira handoff. This is where FSAD breaks the handoff chain. spec.md design-decisions.md AGENTS.md Phase 3 — Implementation Planning & Task Decomposition The Engineer feeds the spec to an AI agent in "plan mode" (read-only). The agent analyzes the codebase, generates an implementation plan, and decomposes work into discrete, parallelizable tasks. The human reviews the plan against the spec — catching hallucinations, missed edge cases, and architectural misalignment before any code is written. plan.md tasks/*.md test-plan.md Phase 4 — Parallel Agent Execution Multiple AI agents execute tasks simultaneously in isolated git worktrees. Each agent works against the spec as its source of truth. A Coordinator agent (or human) routes tasks, and a Verifier agent checks eac

title: Small Teams, Shared Context
label: 03 — The FSAD Pod
text: 03 — The FSAD Pod Small Teams, Shared Context The Markdown is the Meeting In FSAD, the spec.md file replaces most of the ceremony of traditional development — the Jira tickets, the Figma handoffs, the sprint planning debates, the slack threads asking "what did we decide?" PM contributes user intent, business constraints, success metrics, and acceptance criteria directly into the spec. UX Designer contributes interaction patterns, component decisions, layout descriptions, and accessibility requirements — inline, not as a separate Figma file. Engineer contributes technical constraints, data models, API contracts, and architecture decisions — and validates feasibility in real-time. AI Agents consume the spec and execute implementation in parallel — the "workforce" that the pod directs.

title: Two Worlds Compared
label: 05 — FSAD vs. Traditional Agile/Scrum
text: 05 — FSAD vs. Traditional Agile/Scrum Two Worlds Compared FSAD doesn't reject Agile values — it fulfills them by removing the ceremony that slowed teams down. Traditional Agile/Scrum — Feature Delivery Sprint Planning Design Handoff Development QA Deploy Planning Design & Handoff Development QA Deploy Typical: 2–4 weeks per feature FSAD — Feature Delivery Live Spec Session (Pod) Plan Agent Execution ∥ Review & Ship Collaborative Spec (PM+UX+Eng) Agent Plan + Parallel Execution Human Review Typical: 1–3 days per feature Dimension Traditional Agile / Scrum FSAD Source of Truth Jira tickets, Confluence docs, Figma files — scattered across tools. Often outdated or conflicting. A single spec.md in the repo. Version-controlled, diff-friendly, always current. Team Structure Separate PM, design, and engineering functions. Handoffs between roles. Scrum team of 5–9. Cross-functional pod of 2–4. PM, UX, and Engineer co-author the spec in the same session. Planning Cadence Sprint planning every 2 weeks. Backlog grooming. Story point estimation. Daily standups. Continuous flow. Features specced, planned, and executed in hours to days. No sprint boundaries. Design Process UX creates mockups in Figma → handoff → engineers interpret → back-and-forth. UX writes design decisions directly into the spec. Agents consume them as instructions. Code Generation Engineers manually write all code. Speed limited by human throughput. AI agents generate code from spec in parallel. Engineers review and verify. Cycle Time 2–4 week sprints. Features may span multiple sprints. Hours to days. Spec-to-deployment loop measured in hours. Knowledge Retention Decisions live in Slack threads, meeting notes, people's heads. Every decision captured in markdown files committed to the repo. Quality Assurance Separate QA phase. Manual + automated tests written by engineers. Tests generated alongside code from spec acceptance criteria. QA is embedded. Role of Engineers Primary code authors. Value = lines of code

title: The Advantages
label: 06 — Why FSAD Wins
text: 06 — Why FSAD Wins The Advantages Cycle Time Compression Eliminating handoffs and delegating implementation to parallel agents compresses 2–4 week sprints into 1–3 days. No Handoff Latency No more Figma → Jira → Slack → Code chain. Design decisions reach code without translation loss. Parallel Execution Multiple agents in isolated worktrees implement different parts of the spec simultaneously. Single Source of Truth spec.md replaces the constellation of Jira, Confluence, Figma, Slack threads, and meeting notes. Knowledge Compound Better specs produce better agent output, which produces cleaner codebases, which produces even better agent output. A virtuous cycle. Democratized Contribution PMs and designers contribute directly to the artifact that drives implementation. No code required.

title: Strengths & Challenges
label: 07 — Honest Tradeoffs
text: 07 — Honest Tradeoffs Strengths & Challenges FSAD ✦ Strengths Radical Cycle Time Reduction Compresses spec-to-ship from weeks to days via agent parallelism. Eliminates Interpretation Drift The spec humans validate is the same artifact agents read. Scales Without Headcount A 3-person pod outputs at the rate of a 10–15 person traditional team. Built-in Institutional Knowledge Specs and decision logs live in the repo. Onboarding = reading markdown. Higher-Quality First Drafts Agent-generated code from structured specs is more consistent than code under sprint pressure. ✦ Challenges High Spec Quality Bar Garbage in, garbage out. Vague specs produce hallucinated code. Non-Deterministic Agents Agents can ignore, duplicate, or over-interpret specs. Human review is critical. Cultural Shift Required Engineers shift to orchestration; PMs and designers must learn structured markdown. Tooling Is Maturing The ecosystem evolves rapidly. Teams must stay current. Not for All Problems Novel research and deeply creative work still require human coding. Traditional Agile/Scrum ✦ Strengths Battle-Tested Decades of refinement. Clear roles, ceremonies, massive training ecosystem. Predictable Cadence Sprint rhythm gives stakeholders reliable forecasting. Human Craftsmanship Engineers deeply understand code they write. No black-box risk. No AI Dependency Works without AI tooling, model quality, or spec-writing discipline. ✦ Challenges Handoff Overhead PM → Design → Engineering chain introduces latency and lost context. Ceremony Overhead Planning, grooming, standups, retros consume hours without producing value. Brooks's Law Adding engineers adds communication overhead. Doesn't scale linearly. Knowledge Trapped in People Context leaves when team members leave.

title: FSAD is not post-Agile. It's Agile fulfilled.
label: The Bottom Line
text: The Bottom Line FSAD is not post-Agile. It's Agile fulfilled. The Agile Manifesto valued "individuals and interactions over processes and tools" and "working software over comprehensive documentation." FSAD delivers on both — by making the spec a live interaction between individuals, and by compiling that spec into working software through AI agents in hours, not weeks.

title: Compositions That Don't Work
label: 03 — Pod Anti-Patterns
text: 03 — Pod Anti-Patterns Compositions That Don't Work 🚫 The Solo Hero One engineer doing everything. No second perspective means spec blind spots go unchallenged. Agents amplify mistakes at scale. 🚫 The Oversized Pod 5+ humans on a single spec. Communication overhead grows quadratically. Split into two pods with a shared API contract. 🚫 The Handoff Pod PM writes spec → throws to designer → throws to engineer. Same sequential process. If you aren't co-authoring, it's not FSAD. 🚫 The Agent-Only Pod Fully autonomous agents, no human review. Agent reliability is non-deterministic. Every pod requires human validation gates. 🚫 The Part-Time Pod Members at 20% allocation across multiple pods. FSAD's speed comes from real-time collaboration. Async stalls the spec session. 🚫 The Duplicate Pod Two engineers with identical skills. The second must own a distinct domain — otherwise use a Triad and let agents parallelize.

title: 5 Habits to Never Hit Your Token Limits
label: 01 — Token Management
text: 01 — Token Management 5 Habits to Never Hit Your Token Limits Every new Claude Code turn re-sends your full conversation history as input tokens. Context accumulates — so later turns grow more expensive and model accuracy starts to degrade well before you hit the limit. These habits slow that growth. 1 Compact at 50% Run /compact when your context reaches ~50% full — accuracy and consistency start degrading around the halfway mark, not at the limit. Compacting early eliminates old tool outputs, summarises decisions already made, and reduces the history re-sent on every new turn. 2 Name the Exact File Reference the specific file, not the directory. A targeted single-file read is orders of magnitude cheaper than recursive folder exploration — and gives the model only what it actually needs, not everything that happens to be nearby. ✓ src/auth/handler.ts ✗ src/auth/ 3 Order Matters After a compact, old messages cost more to carry than new ones. Re-state the file you need immediately after compacting so Claude doesn't have to re-read it from the summarised history. Name the resource first; ask the question second. 4 Plan Before You Build Ask for a plan first, review it, then ask for the implementation. A single planning round costs a fraction of a failed multi-step implementation. One focused task per session beats five interleaved ones. research → plan → implement 5 End Each Task with /compact Before switching to a new task in the same session, run /compact to summarise and discard the completed work's context. Carry-over messages from a finished task inflate the window for the next one — even if that context is no longer relevant. compact between tasks one job per context

title: Match Effort to the Task
label: 02 — Effort Calibration
text: 02 — Effort Calibration Match Effort to the Task Claude Code's effort setting controls how deeply it reasons before responding. Over-efforting simple tasks wastes tokens; under-efforting complex ones produces shallow work. low / medium Quick asks, formatting, simple refactors, and boilerplate. Use when the task requires no sustained reasoning chain. rename a variable format JSON add a comment high default on Opus Real coding, debugging, and refactoring. The right setting for most daily FSAD work — deep enough to reason about dependencies without burning tokens on simpler tasks. feature implementation bug fix refactor xhigh / max Complex architectures, hard cross-cutting bugs, and novel problems with no clear prior. Reserve for tasks where the cost of a shallow answer is high. system design security audit hard debugging Quick reference Effort commands /effort low # exploration, quick questions /effort medium # default on Sonnet; most lightweight tasks /effort high # default on Opus; standard daily FSAD work /effort xhigh # deep reasoning, slower output /effort max # maximum reasoning budget Effort persists for the session. Reset it explicitly when switching task types — e.g. drop back to /effort medium after a hard debugging session to avoid over-spending on a simple rename.

title: Set Once, Forget
label: 03 — Session Hygiene
text: 03 — Session Hygiene Set Once, Forget Things you should configure once so you never have to repeat them in a prompt. Every repetition is a token cost and a cognitive tax. Pattern 1 Write a CLAUDE.md Any behavior you find yourself re-stating each session belongs in CLAUDE.md . The model loads it at the start of every session — you never have to say it again. ## Constraints - Never add comments explaining what the code does. - Always run the build script before committing. - Use TypeScript strict mode; no `any`. - Ask before running destructive git commands. Scope it to the project: repo-level CLAUDE.md for project conventions, ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for personal habits that apply everywhere. Nested CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories load on-demand when Claude works in that directory. Pattern 2 Problem First, Code Second Always describe the problem before asking for code. "Here's what's broken and why it matters" is cheaper than three rounds of rejected implementations because the model guessed wrong about the goal. ✓ explain the problem ✓ share the constraint ✗ jump straight to "write me..." Pattern 3 Right Tool for the Depth Don't use dynamic workflows ( ultracode ) for anything a single focused session can do. Spawning 20 agents to rename a variable costs 20× and delivers the same answer. Reserve multi-agent orchestration for genuinely parallelisable work. single-agent default multi-agent for parallel scope Pattern 4 Use Hooks for Repeating Checks If you always want something checked before or after a tool call (e.g. lint after every file write, confirm before destructive git commands), encode it as a hook — not a prompt instruction that silently disappears after /compact . "hooks": { "PostToolUse": [{ "matcher": "Write", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "npm run lint"}] }] } Hooks are shell commands wired to lifecycle events — they fire regardless of what's in context. Instruction files ( CLAUDE.md , .claude/rules/ ) are re-injected after /compact automaticall

text: performance-reviewer lite ▼ Primary scope Algorithmic efficiency, resource consumption, and concurrency performance. Algorithmic complexity — O(n²) or worse where O(n log n) or better exists, nested loops over large collections, redundant iteration. Database / storage patterns — N+1 query patterns, missing indexes on filtered/sorted columns, unbounded fetches without pagination. Memory — unnecessary allocations in hot paths, string concatenation in loops, large data structures kept in memory when streaming would suffice. I/O — blocking I/O on the main thread, synchronous disk reads in request handlers, missing batching or buffering, missing connection pooling. Caching — expensive computations repeated without caching, cache invalidation that's too aggressive or not aggressive enough. label: 09.5 — The Claude Configuration Cascade
text: 09.5 — The Claude Configuration Cascade How Teams Structure .claude/ Across Org, Project & Developer Layers CLAUDE.md and .claude/ aren't just one file in one folder — they cascade. Org-wide rules, project-specific context, and personal preferences compose automatically as Claude walks up the directory tree. Here's how to architect the layers so team-shared rules stay in git, personal preferences stay local, and nothing gets duplicated. The .claude/ directory (project layer) .claude/ at project root · committed to git · shared with team The project-level .claude/ folder is the control center for Claude Code. It defines instructions, custom commands, permission rules, and specialized agent behaviors for everyone working in the repo. CLAUDE.md Central instruction manual. Claude reads it at session start for project context, architecture, and coding standards. settings.json Permission controls — which tools (bash, read, write) are allowed, which files or commands are denied, which MCP servers are available. rules/ Modular, markdown-based instructions. Rules without a paths field apply globally; others only when working in designated directories. commands/ Custom slash commands (e.g. /project:review ). Each markdown file becomes a command, with shell support via the ! prefix. skills/ Reusable, context-aware workflows. More advanced than commands — auto-invoked by Claude when relevant, not just triggered manually. agents/ Specialized subagents with defined personas and restricted tool access. Run risky tasks (reviews, audits) in isolated sessions. The ~/.claude/ directory (user layer) ~/.claude/ · personal to each developer · never committed to git The global folder holds personal preferences that apply across every project on your machine. title: Lessons from Real-World FSAD Adoption
label: 12 — Best Practices & Guidelines
text: 12 — Best Practices & Guidelines Lessons from Real-World FSAD Adoption Practical guidance for teams adopting spec-driven agentic development. Background Context Matters Avoid over-emphasis on technical capabilities. Insufficient business context hurts initial coding sessions. A holistic approach beyond engineering-only specifications yields best results. Include background details, business context, problems to be solved, and design systems. Prompting Be Specific About What, Not How Tell Claude what outcome you want, not the implementation steps. Let the agent choose the approach based on codebase context. Provide Business Context Include business requirements, constraints, and existing patterns. "We need a user preferences API because mobile users complain about notification noise" is better than "add a PATCH endpoint." Use @ References Point Claude at specific files with @filename . This ensures the right context is loaded and prevents the agent from searching in the wrong places. Use Plan Mode First For complex features, start with --conversation-mode plan . Let Claude analyze and propose before making changes. Review the plan, then execute. Project Structure Keep CLAUDE.md Concise Under 100 lines. If it's too long, Claude may miss critical rules. Move detailed docs to docs/ for progressive loading. Use Local CLAUDE.md Files Place module-specific rules near the code they protect. src/auth/CLAUDE.md gets loaded when Claude works in that directory. Organize docs/ for Progressive Context Architecture overview, ADRs, and runbooks in docs/ . Claude reads them when relevant, not every session. Version Control Your Prompts Specs, skills, and configuration are code. Commit them. Review changes in PRs. Roll back if something breaks. Workflow Use /clear Between Tasks Reset context between unrelated tasks. Stale context from a previous task can mislead agents on the current one. Use /compact When Context Gets Large Compress conversation history to free up context window spa

text: Dynamic Workflows — Parallel Multi-Agent Orchestration ▼ Dynamic workflows run tens to hundreds of parallel subagents in a single session — tackling problems too large for a single-pass solution. Available on Max, Team, and Enterprise plans . On Enterprise, off by default at launch — admins enable via Claude Code settings. Trigger keyword: ultracode Type the word ultracode in the prompt input (it highlights violet) to let Claude decide when to run a full dynamic workflow automatically. Press Alt+W or Backspace immediately after the keyword appears to dismiss an accidental trigger. To disable the keyword entirely, go to /config → Workflow keyword trigger . (v2.1.160) The built-in workflow prompt keyword uses a purple shimmer highlight and only fires on explicit phrases like "run a workflow" or "workflow:" — casual mentions of "workflow" in conversation no longer trigger it, reducing accidental activations (v2.1.178).

title: Subprocess Sandboxing
label: 14 — Claude Power Usage
text: Subprocess Sandboxing ▼ Claude Code supports OS-level sandboxing that restricts what Bash subprocesses can read, write, and reach on the network — enforced by Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux / WSL2. Run /sandbox to enable it and choose a mode. Linux and WSL2 users must first install the required packages: sudo apt-get install bubblewrap socat (Ubuntu/Debian) or sudo dnf install bubblewrap socat (Fedora). Sandbox modes Mode Behavior Auto-allow Sandboxed bash commands run automatically without approval prompts. Commands that cannot be sandboxed (e.g. need access to non-allowed network hosts) fall back to the normal permission flow. rm targeting critical paths still prompts. Regular permissions All bash commands go through the standard permission flow even when sandboxed — more control, more prompts. The sandbox still enforces the same filesystem and network boundaries. Key settings.json keys Setting key Effect sandbox.enabled Enable sandboxing ( true / false ). Equivalent to using /sandbox interactively. sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite Array of paths (absolute, ~/ , or ./ relative to project) that subprocess commands may write to outside the working directory — e.g. ["~/.kube", "/tmp/build"] . Arrays merge across config scopes. sandbox.filesystem.denyRead Block subprocess read access to specified paths — e.g. ["~/"] to prevent reading outside the project. sandbox.filesystem.allowRead Re-allow reads within a denyRead region — e.g. ["."] to permit the current project while blocking the rest of ~/ . sandbox.network.allowedDomains Allowlist of domains Bash subprocesses may reach. New domain requests trigger a permission prompt; use allowManagedDomainsOnly: true to block unapproved domains automatically. sandbox.network.deniedDomains Block specific domains even when an allowedDomains wildcard would otherwise permit them — useful for blocking telemetry or third-party endpoints in CI. sandbox.failIfUnavailable Set to true to make sandbox startup failure a hard error

title: Prompt Caching & KV Cache
label: 14 — Claude Power Usage
text: Prompt Caching & KV Cache ▼ Claude maintains a key-value (KV) cache of computed attention states for the leading prefix of each conversation. When a new request shares the same prefix as a cached one, Claude skips recomputing that prefix — delivering faster responses at roughly 10% of the regular input-token cost for cached tokens. The cache is prefix-based: content must appear at the beginning of the prompt to be cacheable. The first matching request in a window incurs a small cache-write overhead; every subsequent request within the TTL window is a cheap cache read. What gets cached in a Claude Code session System prompt injected by Claude Code at session start CLAUDE.md files loaded from the project and user config Large read-only documents attached at the top of the conversation Accumulated conversation history prefix (up to the last assistant turn) TTL configuration Env Var Effect ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H=1 Opt into 1-hour prompt cache TTL (API key, Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry). Improves hit rate for long or repeated sessions. FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M=1 Force 5-minute TTL regardless of other settings. Choosing your TTL TTL Best for 5 min (default) Short one-off sessions; acceptable when sessions rarely outlast 5 minutes; lowest storage overhead. 1 hour Long coding sessions, nightly CI pipelines, any workflow where Claude re-reads the same large codebase context repeatedly. Enable whenever a session is likely to outlast 5 minutes or runs on a schedule. title: Exit Codes & Decision Control
label: 15 — Hooks
text: Exit Codes & Decision Control ▼ Exit codes determine whether a hook blocks execution or just logs a warning. Getting this right is critical for policy enforcement. Exit Code Behavior 0 Success — stdout parsed for JSON output. Most events: written to debug log. Exceptions: UserPromptSubmit and SessionStart show stdout as context. 2 Blocking error — blocks tool call, rejects prompt, prevents stop, or blocks compaction (depending on event). Stderr is fed back as the error message. Any other Non-blocking error — stderr shown as warning in transcript. Execution continues normally. Exit 2 Is the Only Blocking Code Exit 1 is non-blocking — it logs an error but doesn't stop anything. You must use exit 2 to enforce policy. This is the most common mistake when writing hooks. PreToolUse permission decisions — control what happens to the tool call: Decision Effect allow Skip permission prompt, execute immediately deny Block the tool call entirely ask Prompt the user to confirm defer Pause for later (non-interactive -p mode only) When multiple hooks fire, precedence is: deny > defer > ask > allow . PreCompact blocking — prevent context compaction from running: Method Effect Exit with code 2 Block compaction; stderr shown as reason Return {"decision":"block"} Block compaction via JSON decision output PostToolUse output replacement — replace the tool's output before Claude sees it: { "hookSpecificOutput": { "updatedToolOutput": "Sanitized or transformed output here" } } Return this JSON from a PostToolUse hook (exit 0) to substitute the tool result Claude receives. Works for all tools — use it to redact sensitive output, normalize formats, or inject additional context. PostToolUse continueOnBlock — soft block: feed the rejection reason back to Claude instead of ending the turn: { "hooks": { "PostToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": ".claude/hooks/check-output.sh", "continueOnBlock": true } ] } ] } } When "continueOnBlock": true is set, a hook

Codex CLI ──▶ MCP Protocol ──▶ JIRA ──▶ Figma ──▶ Notion ──▶ Azure DevOps ──▶ Google Workspace Setting Up MCP Connections via codex mcp Codex uses the codex mcp CLI to manage MCP servers. For HTTP servers (Jira, Figma, Notion), use --url . For stdio servers (Azure DevOps, community tools), pass the command after -- . 1 Add an MCP Server Use codex mcp add to register a server. title: Built-in Code Review with /review
label: 04 — Code Review
text: 04 — Code Review Built-in Code Review with /review Codex includes a native code review command that analyzes diffs without modifying your code. How /review Works The /review slash command analyzes your current diff (staged and unstaged changes) and provides feedback on bugs, security issues, code quality, and style — without making any modifications to your files. Usage 1 Start a Codex Session Launch Codex in your project directory: codex 2 Run /review Type /review to analyze your current changes. Codex examines the diff and provides structured feedback: # Review current working tree changes /review # Or ask for a specific review focus "Review the changes in src/auth/ for security issues" 3 Act on Feedback Review the findings and ask Codex to fix specific issues, or continue working on your own. Claude Code Comparison Claude Code uses a multi-agent fleet for code review (multiple specialized agents in parallel). Codex's /review is single-agent by default but can leverage multi-agent threads if configured. Both approaches catch bugs — Claude's is more comprehensive, Codex's is faster for quick reviews.

title: Turn Repeatable Workflows into Reusable Expert Modes
label: 05 — Building Skills
text: 05 — Building Skills Turn Repeatable Workflows into Reusable Expert Modes Codex skills are markdown-driven workflows stored in .agents/skills/ — each skill gets its own directory with a SKILL.md file. What are Codex Skills? Skills are markdown instructions that Codex follows when invoked. Unlike Claude's flat .claude/skills/ files, Codex skills use a directory structure: each skill has a folder containing SKILL.md plus optional scripts, references, and asset files. Skill Directory Structure .agents/skills/ ├── code-review/ │ └── SKILL.md # Skill instructions ├── deploy/ │ ├── SKILL.md # Skill instructions │ ├── scripts/ │ │ └── check-staging.sh # Helper scripts │ └── references/ │ └── deploy-checklist.md └── estimate/ └── SKILL.md Example: Deployment Skill Deploy Skill — SKILL.md ▼ # Deployment Skill ## Overview Guided deployment to staging and production environments. ## Process 1. Run the test suite: `npm test` 2. Check for uncommitted changes: `git status` 3. Run the staging check script: `./scripts/check-staging.sh` 4. Build the production bundle: `npm run build` 5. Deploy to staging: `npm run deploy:staging` 6. Run smoke tests against staging 7. If smoke tests pass, deploy to production ## Safety Rules - NEVER deploy directly to production without staging - Always check the deploy-checklist.md reference - Abort if any test or smoke test fails Best Practice Start with one skill for your most repeated workflow. Codex skills can include shell scripts and reference docs alongside the markdown — use this for deployment checklists, migration procedures, or incident response runbooks.

text: 06 — Guidelines Lessons from Real-World Codex Adoption Practical guidance for teams using Codex for spec-driven agentic development. Prompting Be Specific About What, Not How Tell Codex what outcome you want, not the implementation steps. Let the agent choose the approach based on codebase context. Provide Business Context Include business requirements, constraints, and existing patterns. "We need a user preferences API because mobile users complain about notification noise" is better than "add a PATCH endpoint." Use Tab for File References Press Tab to fuzzy-search files by name (prefix with @ ). This ensures the right context is loaded and prevents Codex from searching in the wrong places. Use /plan Mode First For complex features, start with /plan . Let Codex analyze and propose before making changes. Review the plan, then let it execute. Project Structure Keep AGENTS.md Focused Stay under the 32 KiB limit. Put detailed docs in docs/ for progressive context — don't bloat your project instructions file. Use Skills for Repeatable Workflows If you find yourself giving the same instructions across sessions, encode them as a skill in .agents/skills/ . Use Local AGENTS.md for Sensitive Modules Place small AGENTS.md files near auth, billing, and infrastructure code. Codex sees the guardrails exactly when working in that directory. Use /compact to Manage Context Long conversations eat context. Use /compact to summarize the conversation and free up tokens for the agent to work with. Bloated AGENTS.md Stuffing every rule into AGENTS.md defeats the purpose. Keep it focused on high-level rules; use docs/ and local AGENTS.md for details. title: Hooks — Automation & Guardrails
label: 07 — Hooks
text: 07 — Hooks Hooks — Automation & Guardrails Event-driven shell commands that fire deterministically at specific points in the agent loop. Models forget. Hooks don't. Hooks inject scripts into Codex's agentic loop at named lifecycle events. Unlike instructions in AGENTS.md that the model may or may not follow, hooks always execute when their event triggers — making them ideal for audit logging, policy enforcement, and automated validation. Generally Available — May 2026 Codex Hooks reached General Availability on 2026-05-14. They are production-ready with no feature flag required — [features] codex_hooks = true is the default and stable for use in production pipelines, enterprise environments, and automated workflows. Hook Event Types Event When it fires Can block? Claude Code equivalent SessionStart Session begins or resumes No — adds context only SessionStart UserPromptSubmit User submits a prompt Yes (exit 2) UserPromptSubmit PreToolUse Before Bash, apply_patch , or MCP tool runs; hooks can inject additional context into the turn by returning a context field in JSON output Yes (exit 2 or deny JSON) PreToolUse PermissionRequest When Codex seeks approval (shell escalation, network) Yes — allow / deny PermissionRequest PostToolUse After tool completes (including failed runs) Yes (exit 2 — replaces output) PostToolUse Stop When a turn completes Yes — can request continuation Stop PreCompact Before context compaction runs Yes (exit 2 blocks compaction) PreCompact PostCompact After context compaction completes No PostCompact Configuration Enable hooks with [features] codex_hooks = true (default). Define hooks inline in config.toml or in a separate hooks.json . Project-scoped hooks go in .codex/config.toml and only load in trusted projects. config.toml hook syntax ▼ # ~/.codex/config.toml (global) or .codex/config.toml (project) [features] codex_hooks = true # Fire before every Bash call [[hooks.PreToolUse]] matcher = "^Bash$" [[hooks.PreToolUse.hooks]] type = "command" c

title: CI/CD Integration

text: CI/CD Integration ▼ Use codex exec for headless execution in pipelines. Combine with --json for machine-readable output. # Headless execution — no TUI, streams to stderr codex exec "fix all lint errors and run tests" # JSON Lines output — includes reasoning-token usage codex exec --json "analyze this codebase for security issues" # Structured response with schema enforcement codex exec --output-schema schema.json "list all API endpoints" # Resume a prior session in headless mode — preserves context, enforces schema codex exec resume --output-schema schema.json "continue from last checkpoint" # Autonomous execution via permission profile (replaces deprecated --full-auto) codex exec --approval-mode never "update dependencies and fix breaking changes" # Quiet mode for scripting codex exec -q "generate changelog from recent commits" > CHANGELOG.md # Throwaway session (no session history saved) codex exec --ephemeral "check for unused imports"

title: Codex Access Tokens
label: 09 — Power Usage
text: Codex Access Tokens ▼ Codex access tokens let ChatGPT Enterprise workspace members run fully non-interactive Codex workflows without manual browser-based authentication. Tokens carry the user's ChatGPT workspace identity and are ideal for scripts, schedulers, and private CI runners that can't go through an OAuth flow. Who can create tokens: ChatGPT Enterprise workspace owners must first authorize members to generate tokens via the workspace admin settings. Once authorized, members create tokens in their account settings and reference them at runtime. # Set the access token via environment variable export CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN=your-token-here # Non-interactive execution — no browser prompt codex exec --approval-mode never "run all tests and report failures" # Use in a CI runner (GitHub Actions example) env : CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN }} Treat Like an API Key Access tokens grant full Codex execution rights under your workspace identity. Store them in secrets managers (AWS Secrets Manager, GitHub Secrets, HashiCorp Vault) — never commit to version control or log in CI output. Rotate tokens if exposure is suspected. Use cases: nightly background refactors, automated spec-to-code pipelines, private on-premise CI runners that need Codex without a browser session. Pairs well with --approval-mode never permission profiles for fully autonomous runs.

title: Permission Profiles
label: 09 — Power Usage
text: Permission Profiles ▼ Permission profiles replace the old binary sandbox flags with named, reusable policies for filesystem and network access. Define them in ~/.codex/config.toml and apply with --approval-mode or default_permissions . Built-in Profile Filesystem Network :read-only Read everywhere None :workspace Write to project root; deny *.env / *.secrets Restricted :danger-no-sandbox Unrestricted Full Define a custom profile: # ~/.codex/config.toml [permissions.myproject.filesystem.":project_roots"] "." = "write" "**/*.env" = "none" # deny reads of .env files glob_scan_max_depth = 3 [permissions.myproject.network] enabled = true mode = "limited" # Apply as default default_permissions = ":myproject" Enterprise: requirements.toml Admins can enforce which profiles are allowed and deny filesystem paths via requirements.toml — an admin-managed policy file that users cannot override. Install it at a system path or distribute via MDM.

text: /goal Workflows ▼ Persisted goals let you define a long-running objective that survives context compaction. Goals are now discoverable — browse all active goals from the TUI picker. When you resume a session, goals are paused by default so they don't carry over unintended work; opt back in from the picker. Goals show clear validation feedback and support multi-day duration tracking. # In a Codex session — set a persistent goal /goal # TUI picker: Create / Pause / Resume / Clear / Browse all goals # Goal persists across /compact; pauses on resume (opt back in from picker) # Multi-day duration shown in goal status output Goals are ideal for large refactors or multi-day feature work. title: Plugins
label: 09 — Power Usage
text: Plugins ▼ Codex plugins extend the agent with bundled tools, skills, and hooks. Browse the marketplace in the TUI or install from the CLI. Plugins can be scoped globally or to a trusted project. # In the TUI: open the plugin marketplace /plugins # Install a plugin from the marketplace codex plugin install <plugin-name> # Remove a plugin codex plugin remove <plugin-name> # Share a plugin with your workspace codex plugin share <plugin-name> # Sync remote plugin bundles codex plugin sync Plugin scoping: Global ( ~/.codex/ ) — available in every session Project ( .codex/ ) — loaded only in trusted projects Workspace-shared — install once, available to teammates via workspace share link; admin-disabled plugins are flagged in /plugins Plugins can bundle skills ( SKILL.md ), hooks, and tool allowlists in a single installable unit. Plugin-bundled hooks are enabled/disabled via the plugin's configuration. As of v0.130.0, the plugin details view (accessible from /plugins ) shows all bundled hooks alongside skills and tools. As of v0.131.0, plugin workflows gained marketplace CLI commands ( codex plugin share , version-aware publish and checkout), clearer shared-workspace buckets, and plugin hooks are now default-enabled on install. Claude Code Equivalent Codex plugins map to Claude Code's plugin system — both use a marketplace model with skill + hook bundling. The key difference: Codex plugins install via codex plugin install ; Claude plugins install via claude plugin install .

title: Measuring FSAD Success
label: 01 — FSAD Metrics
text: 01 — FSAD Metrics Measuring FSAD Success What to measure to demonstrate the value of agentic development to your organization. Highest Priority Token Consumption by User Track per-developer AI usage to identify adoption patterns and cost centers. High consumption with high output signals effective use; high consumption with low output signals coaching opportunities. Total Monthly Epics / Tickets Volume of work items completed, comparing pre- vs. post-FSAD adoption. Expect a meaningful increase as AI agents accelerate implementation cycles. Total Monthly Story Points Throughput measurement for sprint-over-sprint comparison. Track velocity trends after FSAD adoption to quantify productivity gains. Total PRs / Commits Development velocity indicator. AI-assisted workflows typically produce higher commit frequency with smaller, more focused changesets. Maintenance vs. New Product Development Breakdown of time and code produced by maintenance vs. new product development. Measures whether AI frees engineering capacity for innovation over sustaining work. Total $ Spend by AI Tool Cost tracking per tool (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.) for ROI analysis. Correlate spend against velocity and output metrics to demonstrate return on investment. Other Metrics AI Coding Tools WAU Weekly Active Users across AI coding tools. Measures adoption breadth across the engineering organization. Lines of Code Produced AI-generated vs. human-written code split. Track the ratio over time to understand how AI contribution evolves. AI Commits vs. Acceptance Rates How often AI-generated code is accepted vs. revised. A quality signal — high acceptance rates indicate well-configured agents and effective specs. Start Small Don't instrument everything on day one. Token consumption + story points alone can demonstrate ROI within a single sprint. Add granularity as your FSAD practice matures and leadership asks deeper questions.
